questions.explanation: One pass over the array doing constant work per element: n iterations, so O(n).
Reading an array element by index takes the same time whatever the array's length: O(1).
For each of the n values of i the inner loop runs n times: n · n = n² iterations.
The inner loop runs n-1, n-2, …, 1 times: n(n-1)/2 comparisons in the worst case (no duplicate). Halving n² doesn't change the growth rate, so it is still O(n²).
Each iteration halves the remaining range, so it takes about log₂ n iterations to shrink n elements to one.
n is halved on every iteration, so the loop runs about log₂ n times.
The outer loop doubles i, so it runs about log₂ n times; the inner loop always runs n times. n · log n.
JavaScript engines implement sort with comparison sorts such as TimSort, which take O(n log n) comparisons.

Every call makes two more calls, and the same values are recomputed over and over. The call tree has roughly 2ⁿ nodes (more precisely about 1.6ⁿ, which is still exponential and usually written O(2ⁿ)).
Each value from 2 to n is computed once and then read from the memo, so there are O(n) calls doing constant work each.
Two loops one after the other: n iterations over a, then m over b. Sequential steps add: O(n + m).
Nested loops multiply: for each of the n elements of a, all m elements of b. Only when both have the same length does it become O(n²).
includes scans the array linearly. Called once per element of a, that's n · n work when both arrays have about n elements. Turning b into a Set first brings it down to O(n).
Building the Set is O(n) and each has() is O(1) on average, so the filter is O(n) as well. O(n) + O(n) = O(n).
indexOf searches from the start of the array each time, up to n steps, and it runs for every element: O(n²). `[...new Set(arr)]` does the same job in O(n).
The loop stops once i² passes n, that is after about √n iterations.
Three nested loops of n iterations each: n · n · n = n³.
The inner loop always runs 10 times, whatever the input. 10n iterations is O(n): a nested loop only makes it quadratic when the inner bound grows with n.
The array is halved log₂ n times, and at each level of the recursion the merges together touch all n elements: O(n) per level × log n levels.
There are n calls, but each one copies the rest of the array with slice: n-1, n-2, … elements. That adds up to about n²/2 copied elements. Passing an index instead of slicing makes it O(n).
Each call halves the exponent and calls itself once (the result is reused for both factors), so there are about log₂ n calls.
Any factor above √n pairs with one below it, so trying divisors up to √n is enough: about √n iterations when n is prime.
Every one of the n × n cells is visited once: n² iterations.
The two pointers meet in the middle after n/2 steps: O(n).
One pass, and Map get/set are O(1) on average: O(n) overall.
The inner loop runs 1 + 2 + 4 + … + (largest power of 2 below n) times. That geometric series is less than 2n, so the total is O(n), not O(n log n).
Euclid's algorithm: every two steps the remainder at least halves, so the number of steps is logarithmic in the smaller number.
n² result cells, each a sum of n products: n³ multiplications.
Each call branches into two calls until depth n (skip the element or take it), so the call tree has 2ⁿ leaves and about 2ⁿ⁺¹ calls in total.
A call on k elements makes k calls on k-1 elements, so there are about n! calls at the bottom and fewer above. Each call also copies its array (O(n) work), which gives O(n · n!).
A single pass that keeps the lowest price so far. Trying every buy/sell pair would be O(n²); this is O(n).
Only a fixed number of variables, however long the array: O(1) extra space.
map builds a new array of n elements, and the returned value counts: O(n).
Each call waits on the next one, so n frames are on the call stack at the deepest point. JavaScript engines don't eliminate tail calls in practice, so this is O(n) stack space.
The iterative version keeps only three indices: O(1).
Same steps as the loop, but each halving adds a stack frame: about log₂ n frames at the deepest point.
An n × n grid holds n² cells.
The time is exponential, but space only depends on how deep the stack gets. fib(n-2) starts after fib(n-1) has returned, so at most n frames are alive at once: O(n).
The memo holds up to n entries and the stack is up to n frames deep: O(n) + O(n) = O(n).
The Set may hold up to n values (when they are all different), even though only a number is returned.

At any moment the live copies are those along one path of the recursion: n/2 + n/4 + … ≤ n, plus the n-element output, and log n stack frames. That's O(n). Copies from finished calls can be garbage-collected.
Elements are swapped inside the input array, and only two indices are kept: O(1) extra space. (The tiny temporary arrays for the swap are constant size.)
The result holds n(n-1)/2 pairs: O(n²).
There are 2ⁿ subsets and each holds up to n elements (n/2 on average), so the result takes O(n · 2ⁿ) space.
The counts array always has 26 slots, however long the word is: constant space, O(1). (Counting the lowercased copy of the word would make it O(n), which is why the question sets it aside.)

At the deepest point there are n frames, and each still holds its slice of n-1, n-2, …, 1 elements. Those copies are all alive at once: about n²/2 elements. With an index parameter it's O(n) stack and no copies.
The parts array and the returned string each hold n characters: O(n).
The loop runs log n times but reuses the same two variables: O(1) space. Time and space are separate questions.
The new array holds every element of both inputs: n + m.
The stack holds one frame per level on the current path, so space grows with the tree's height h: O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a degenerate one that is a linked list.
